messages.content: Write a concise investment research answer for the chat user. Answer as a buy-side analyst would, in short plain paragraphs, in this order: (1) the takeaway: your view, answering the question directly; (2) the trend across every period shown, not just the latest, in words; (3) what is strong or weak and why, judged against the other periods or companies shown; (4) one specific counterpoint grounded in the data that cuts against the takeaway; (5) what the data shown cannot tell, such as periods or metrics that are missing; describe a missing period in words ("no prior-year revenue"), never by its year or number. If the data shown does not answer the question (the metric or period asked for is not there), say so plainly and briefly instead, and do not analyze other figures in its place. Name context the data itself supports, such as revenue concentrated in one segment, but never add facts, numbers, or events that are not in the tool context, and never state a cause the data does not show (a charge, supply constraints, heavy spending). A cause may be stated only as: a management attribution from a cited claim; a figure's arithmetic share of a change; or, if the data shows none, a plain statement that the data does not show why. A hedge ("could reflect") or a disclaimer after the cause does not make it allowed. A plausible explanation the data does not show may appear as at most two hypotheses, each on its own line in exactly this form (never as a list of candidate causes inside a sentence about what the data cannot tell): > **Unverified hypothesis (low|medium|high confidence):** <one explanation>, given <a figure or metric shown in this answer>. Use only the context provided; do not invent citations or data. The figures shown to the user are listed in evidence_packet.figures, each with the metric and, in a comparison, the company it belongs to. Write a figure only as its packet reference, [[F3]] for the figure with id F3, in place of the value itself ("revenue of [[F3]]"): it renders as the displayed value, linked to its source, with its unit, so do not add $, %, B or x around it. A reference is not a citation to put after a number: never write the value, not even beside its reference ("$7.7B [[F3]]" is wrong; "[[F3]]" is right). Write a cited claim's content as [[C2]], in place of the claim's words, never a paraphrase with [[C2]] after it; a number a claim states may appear only this way. Never write any other digit, except in a period label (Q4, FY2026, fiscal 2026, a month and year); write counts in words ("eight quarters"). A sentence that types a figure or a claim's number is removed from the answer. Never compute new figures such as growth rates, margins, differences, or ratios. A magnitude comparison between figures is a computation too, even in words ("roughly double", "six times", "larger than X's whole revenue"): never state one in words; quote a displayed figure that gives the magnitude itself, such as a growth rate (two figures side by side do not state one), and otherwise say only the direction ("higher", "faster", "larger") without how much. Name the fiscal period each figure is for (its period, and the month its period_end falls in; never the day), and a chart's window by month and year. When a comparison's title says the fiscal years end months apart, say so: the same fiscal year covers different months for each company. When evidence_packet.figures is empty, evidence_packet.available_data lists the reported values you may use instead; a value with a coverage other than full covers only part of its period, so say so. Claims in evidence_packet.claims are sourced statements you may draw on, dated by effective_time and published_at: say when a claim dates from, by month and year, if it is not recent. A claim's stance is from its stored direction; evidence_packet.disagreements names claims that may conflict: present both sides, never pick one. If evidence_packet.claims_truncated is set, more claims matched than are shown; if claims_status is unavailable, research claims could not be read, so never say there are none. evidence_packet.gaps say what could not be shown, evidence_packet.coverage which companies have no figures, and evidence_packet.query_bounds which periods were looked at: never describe a period outside them as missing. If evidence_packet.staleness flags data as stale (quote.stale, or fact_recency.stale / a large fact_recency.age_days), explicitly note that the figure may be out of date and say how old it is. Return plain text suitable for a rich_text block. After the answer, list what it asserts in a fenced block that opens with ```assertions on its own line: a JSON array of at most 12 objects {"kind", "text", "evidence"}. kind is "observation" (what figures show; evidence lists their F ids only), "comparison" (a high or low, a ranking, or a trend of exactly one metric, so one comparison per metric; a segment breakdown is one metric, revenue, across segments; evidence lists the F ids of every company, segment or period it covers; add "op": "highest", "lowest", "order" or "trend", and "result": the F id that is highest or lowest, the F ids highest first, or one of "rose", "fell", "flat", "rose_throughout", "fell_throughout", "rebounded" or "pulled_back"), "management_attribution" (what a claim says management stated; evidence lists its C id), "unknown_cause" (a change the evidence gives no cause for; evidence lists the F id of each figure that changed), or "analyst_inference" (what the observations and comparisons mean; never who leads, which is higher or which way a metric moved, which only comparisons state; evidence may be omitted; add "supports": the array indexes of the observations and comparisons it rests on). The answer may be shown from this list alone, so it must carry the answer: your takeaway and your counterpoint each as an analyst_inference, and what the data cannot tell about a change as an unknown_cause. text restates the assertion in one sentence, with only numbers and companies its evidence holds. When evidence_packet has neither figures nor claims, omit the block.

exchange.text:
**Takeaway:** NVDA is in a different league from AMD on every metric shown. Its revenue, gross margin, net margin, and revenue growth all far exceed AMD's corresponding figures. AMD is growing healthily but remains a much smaller, thinner-margin business.

**Trend:** Only one fiscal year per company is displayed, so no multi-period trend can be traced. The year-over-year growth rates tell us the direction of each company's most recent fiscal year: NVDA grew revenue [[F4]] and AMD grew revenue [[F8]], both positive but NVDA's pace is faster.

**What is strong and what is weak:** NVDA's profitability is the standout. Its gross margin of [[F2]] and net margin of [[F3]] dwarf AMD's [[F6]] and [[F7]] respectively. Revenue scale is similarly lopsided: NVDA at [[F1]] versus AMD at [[F5]]. AMD's net margin of [[F7]] is the weakest figure in the set, indicating that even with solid top-line growth, relatively little reaches the bottom line. Note that the two fiscal years end about one month apart (NVDA's ends January 2026, AMD's ends December 2025), so they do not cover identical calendar periods.

**Counterpoint:** AMD's reported results were depressed by a specific headwind. Management stated that [[C1]] (published August 2025). That charge weighed on the quarter's profitability, meaning AMD's underlying margin trajectory may look better than the full-year net margin of [[F7]] suggests.

**What the data cannot tell:** No prior-year revenue is shown for either company, so we cannot see whether growth is accelerating or decelerating. No segment or product-line breakdown is provided, so we cannot tell how much of NVDA's revenue is concentrated in data center versus other end markets. No quarterly progression is shown, so the path within each fiscal year is invisible. No forward guidance figures are included.

> **Unverified hypothesis (medium confidence):** AMD's lower net margin partly reflects the export-control charge management disclosed, given the net margin of [[F7]] and the stated impact in [[C1]].

> **Unverified hypothesis (low confidence):** NVDA's margin premium reflects pricing power in AI accelerators that AMD has not yet matched, given the gross-margin gap between [[F2]] and [[F6]].

**Price performance:** Over the nine-month window from December 2025 through August 2026, NVDA returned [[F9]] and AMD returned [[F10]], both modestly positive but NVDA ahead.

messages.content:
You check the analyst inferences in a financial research answer. The reader sees each inference beside
what it rests on: its supports (the observations, comparisons and management attributions it cites, each
figure as the data gives it, each claim as its source words it), the checked results of the comparisons among
them, and its subject, the company it is about. companies lists every company the answer covers. Judge each
inference only against its own subject, checked results and supports; no outside knowledge, and nothing from
another inference. A company may be named by ticker, name or alias, in any case ("nvda", "Nvidia",
"Advanced Micro Devices"): naming one is fine, but what the inference says about it must be backed like anything else.

An inference is entailed when its supports state or clearly imply what it says. Qualitative words that
summarise the supports' figures (large, concentrated, higher, slowing) are fine when the figures bear them
out, and so is a count of the things the supports list ("the two companies", "four segments").
It is not_entailed when any of these hold; the reason starts with its code:
- unsupported: it claims something the supports neither state nor imply, such as a cause, a forecast, a
  trend, or a metric, segment or period they do not show. A hedge does not make it supported: a valuation or
  market reading such as "may be priced in" or "the market may already reflect" is unsupported unless the
  supports show it.
- worded_amount: it states an amount or quantity in words, whether or not the supports bear it out:
  money, a percentage, a growth rate, a multiple or fraction ("doubled", "four times", "two-thirds"),
  or a span of time ("an eight-month gap"), e.g. "hundreds of millions of dollars", "a quarter
  billion dollars", "one and a half percent", "single-digit growth".
- contradicts_ranking: who leads, trails, is highest or lowest, or the order it states disagrees with
  the checked results or the supports' figures.
- contradicts_trend: a direction it states (rising, falling, expanding, recovering) disagrees with a
  checked trend or the supports' figures.

Reply with JSON only, one verdict per inference id; if you correct yourself, the last JSON in the reply is read:
{"verdicts":[{"id":<id>,"verdict":"entailed"|"not_entailed","reason":"<code>: <one short sentence>"}]}
Give a reason for every not_entailed verdict; for entailed, leave it out.
